kp.k: Cloud infrastructure underpins Aderant's AI automation strategy
kp.d: Cartrett presents cloud migration as enabling simpler updates, AI deployment and automation of manual law-firm business tasks. He recalls nine applications incorporating Maddy AI launched the previous year and reports four more AI applications already launched in 2025. These are vendor-reported releases; his vision of one-touch time entry flowing through billing is a projected benefit.
qs: the reason for the cloud more than anything else is just what you can do within the technology, the simplification of how we can roll out new features and updates.
I think we rolled out nine new applications that included some type of Maddy AI in them. Already this year, we've rolled out four more applications that have AI.
literally go into one-touch time that basically flows all the way through to a bill going out the door

kp.k: Customization and risk aversion slow cloud migration
kp.d: Cartrett acknowledges migration has been slower than initially desired, grading progress B. He attributes customer hesitation to extensive firm-specific billing customizations and historically burdensome upgrade testing. He promises continued on-premises support and considers any compulsory migration distant, while making some new AI-enabled capabilities conditional on cloud identity. He expects three AmLaw 50 firms to be live in Sierra during 2025 and predicts prominent adopters will encourage others.
qs: we have not been able to move, maybe, as fast as we originally wanted to.
Every law firm needs something different. So you can understand where there's that hesitancy.
we will continue to support our on-prem clients
we can only offer those if you're a part of the Aderant identity, which is only available when you're in the cloud.
I think we have this year, I want to say there's three Amlaw 50 firms that will be live inside Sierra.

kp.k: Customer anecdote suggests faster pre-bill processing
kp.d: Cartrett relays a conference customer story about a thousand-lawyer firm's cloud migration, saying it cut its pre-bill runs in half while producing well over 10,000 pre-bills monthly. He qualifies the account with 'I think'; the transcript provides neither independent measurement nor a precise definition of the reduction.
qs: one of them made the move, a thousand lawyer firm, I think they cut their pre-bill runs in half and their pre-bills were like well in excess of 10,000 a month.

kp.k: Core cloud innovation differs from paid premium automation
kp.d: Cartrett describes Cloud GL and AR as early-adopter releases that do not yet reproduce all legacy functionality, though they add some new capabilities. He projects feature competitiveness around October or November 2025 and describes the target as parity plus. Sierra subscribers receive core improvements without additional payment, whereas heavier cross-system AI automation is offered as paid premium functionality.
qs: we've kind of treated this as the early adopter, this first piece, this is the early adopter piece.
probably by the time we get October, November, you'll be, so, I don't know what the right way of saying this is, you'll be feature competitive of both
for our clients that are in Sierra, this is not something they have to pay for. They get it.
Those premium features are much more heavier, kind of AI automation stuff over the top, that if customers want to subscribe to that, they can also bring that in as well.
That's the only stuff that we're monetizing.

kp.k: Ask Matty targets data queries and customer self-service
kp.d: Cartrett says Ask Matty is intended to answer questions across Aderant's portfolio, replacing the need to assemble answers through reports and separate applications. He describes it as trained on Aderant data structures and predicts its greatest impact will be helping customers troubleshoot and use software independently, rather than only generating answers from their business data.
qs: You should be able to ask an inquiry of anything that you have in the Aderant portfolio directly from Ask Matty.
Ask Matty is nothing more than trained on all the Aderant data the way everything's structured to be able to provide you those same generative answers for whatever your question may be.
besides allowing them the opportunity to generate and create their own answers from their data, is also help them be able to use the product better.
we want to try to shift the entire support experience as far left as humanly possible

kp.k: Agentic workflows could replace fragmented application sequences
kp.d: Cartrett argues that generative AI should extend beyond question-answering to managing complete workflows across formerly separate applications, while retaining human checking. He says Aderant has rolled out agentic architecture and identifies Striden's shared architecture and data plane as the integration mechanism. The account describes strategic direction and enabling infrastructure, not measured autonomous-workflow performance.
qs: too many software companies, us included, we're still thinking in terms of apps.
where we are today with all the agentic models that exist and even our own agentic architecture that we've just rolled out, we should be merging those.
One thing should be able to manage that workflow all the way out the door, with humans obviously being able to check things in the middle of it.
Striden sits as that core architecture. That's where all the AI sits. Every other application is sitting on top of it.
The data plane that exists within Striden, that's what brings all the different products together.

kp.k: Integrated firm workflows require reorganizing vendor support
kp.d: Cartrett argues that increasingly integrated law-firm systems make departmental handoffs between vendor sales, implementation and support inadequate. He describes Chief Client Officer Josiah Chaves's mandate as redesigning products, processes and staff interactions to enable customer independence, including workflow development. He treats organizational structure, training and potentially compensation as necessary complements to product changes, rather than claiming AI alone resolves service problems.
qs: those lines are starting to blend because things are integrating, they're coming from different systems.
when you're constantly getting passed from different departments, that is a horrible experience.
that starts within our product, and then we focus on the processes that we have inside when they do need to reach out, and then the people and how they work and work individually with our clients.
Whether it's the how we organize ourselves, the training, even how some groups are compensated.

kp.k: New analytics address everyday law-firm reporting gaps
kp.d: Cartrett acknowledges that Aderant historically handled very simple and very difficult reporting better than everyday reporting needed by lawyers and other professionals, often relying on partners for the latter. He presents Striden Analytics as filling that gap and reports favorable conference reactions, without supplying adoption or outcome metrics.
qs: we do really hard reporting well. We do really simple reporting well.
But the stuff that to me is like the table stakes that a lawyer and other professionals need on a day-to-day basis. I don't know that we ever really did that really well.
the rolling out of Striden Analytics actually fills a major hole

kp.k: Automated timekeeping shifts lawyers toward reviewing generated entries
kp.d: Cartrett says iTimeKeep Premium generates time cards, narratives and phase/task codes for lawyers to review and release. He predicts this will address firms' difficulty obtaining timely time entries. He describes client engagement rules as governing both time cards and subsequent billing; the transcript does not quantify time savings or error rates.
qs: Now being able to generate a time card, literally create the narrative for you. It also lines up the code, the phase, the task.
you're doing nothing but reviewing it based on the work that you've done that day and then boom, it's released.
Knowing how law firms are always struggling to get lawyers to get time in, I think this is going to be the big change
those actual rules and guidelines are what governs the time card and what happens in billing and out the door.

kp.k: Payment outcome data differentiates integrated billing automation
kp.d: Cartrett argues that Aderant's end-to-end system and BillBlast payment information give it an advantage over standalone automated-time vendors. He says knowing which entries are accepted, rejected and paid lets Aderant suggest narratives and codes aimed at avoiding downstream e-billing rework. This is his competitive claim about billing compliance, not an independently demonstrated improvement or a claim about professional-rule compliance.
qs: our compliance is based entirely upon what you're paid because we know the answer based on what's going on in BillBlast.
I know what gets rejected. I know what is accepted.
great, congratulations, you got the lawyer's time, he's going to be doing it over again anyway.
it then suggests a narrative that we know actually aligns with what's going to get through the door and give them their codes, their phase, their task, everything else with it.

kp.k: Five-year outlook emphasizes capacity rather than job losses
kp.d: Asked about the next five years, Cartrett predicts substantial changes in firm processes as applications and product lines merge. He explicitly rejects anticipated job losses and instead expects workers to accomplish more. These are forecasts, supported by his interpretation of technology direction rather than employment evidence; he contrasts them with the more conventional revenue-growth discussions he heard from firm CIOs and CFOs.
qs: This idea that all of a sudden people are going to lose their jobs, I actually do not believe that.
I do believe somebody doing their job today will be able to do more.
Right now, I've got seven different product lines serving seven different groups, and there's different products under each one of them.
You can already see the handwriting on the wall where these things start to merge.

kp.k: AI efficiencies support fixed fees and pricing experimentation
kp.d: Cartrett reports that a Melbourne firm's CFO required lawyers to use Copilot for basic communications, then converted efficiencies into a fixed-fee offering. His illustration reduces work from 10 hours to 8 and prices it at the equivalent of 9 hours, but he explicitly says the numbers are invented. He also cites an Allen and Overy antitrust subscription service as an example of pricing experimentation, without claiming that AI will necessarily eliminate hourly billing.

I'm just going to make up a number here. Let's say it went from 10 hours down to 8 hours.
they turned around and rolled that out to our clients as a fixed fee for what would have basically been the cost for 9 hours.
whether it's billable hours, whether it's fixed fee, I mean, Allen and Overy just rolled out a subscription service.

He predicts a similar adjustment with AI: some mundane tasks should cease contributing billable hours, while lawyer expertise could still sustain revenue. This is an anecdote-based expectation, not a demonstrated revenue outcome.

kp.k: CEO uses AI for learning and strategic ideation
kp.d: Cartrett reports taking a 20-minute AI class every morning with the aim of building an application. Beyond routine drafting and presentations, he recommends using AI tools to discuss business strategy. He acknowledges that tools often repeat his own thinking but recounts receiving an unfamiliar, useful process suggestion. This is personal experience with managerial augmentation, not evidence of measured decision-quality improvements.

Every time we start pursuing a strategy for something that we're wanting to do in the business, I've caught myself starting to have conversations with different AI tools that I use.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chris Cartrett predicts that AI will integrate law-firm business workflows, automate timekeeping and billing, increase users' self-sufficiency and employee capacity, and support new pricing models without necessarily eliminating jobs or lawyer revenue.
pts.d: Cartrett's claims concern primarily the business of law rather than substantive legal advice. (1) He presents Aderant's cloud platform as enabling AI features and automation that can connect time entry through billing. He predicts that agentic architecture will merge separate applications into end-to-end workflows with human checkpoints. (2) He describes Ask Matty as providing generative answers across Aderant data and helping customers troubleshoot and use software; he expects self-service support to be its greatest impact. (3) He describes iTimeKeep Premium as generating time cards, narratives, codes, phases and tasks for lawyer review. He claims Aderant's access to actual billing acceptance, rejection and payment information gives it an advantage over standalone timekeeping tools: proposed entries can be aligned with engagement guidelines and what gets paid, avoiding downstream rework. He expects this application to have the largest impact on customer firms. (4) Looking five years ahead, he predicts major process changes as product lines merge, but rejects the idea that AI will cause people to lose jobs, instead expecting existing employees to accomplish more. (5) He anticipates multiple pricing approaches, including fixed fees and subscriptions, rather than explicitly predicting the billable hour's demise. He argues that firms can retain revenue while removing mundane work from billable activity because clients ultimately value lawyers' skill. (6) In his own legal-technology business, he describes AI as useful for routine communications, presentations and exploring business strategies.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Cartrett supports his claims with product descriptions, internal deployment experience, customer anecdotes and historical analogy; the interview supplies no measured AI accuracy results or systematic evidence for the employment and market predictions.
pts.d: (1) For platform-enabled automation, Cartrett reports approximately nine applications incorporating Maddy AI released the previous year and four more AI applications released in the interview year, plus an agentic architecture already rolled out. These are reports of product availability, not quantified workflow outcomes. He also recalls an unnamed thousand-lawyer firm's pre-bill runs being cut in half after migration, with more than 10,000 monthly pre-bills; that anecdote concerns cloud migration and is not identified as an isolated AI effect. (2) For Ask Matty, he explains its access to structured Aderant data and support knowledge, but offers no measured reduction in support contacts or verified answer-quality results. (3) For timekeeping, he cites the end-to-end system's engagement rules and BillBlast payment information as the mechanism underpinning the claimed advantage. No comparative rejection rates, collection improvements or time savings are supplied. (4) For pricing adaptation, he recounts an unnamed Melbourne firm's mandated Copilot use followed by fixed-fee packaging. He explicitly invents the numerical illustration: work falling from ten to eight hours and being priced at nine hours is not reported study data. He also mentions an Allen and Overy antitrust subscription offering as an example of pricing variety, without establishing AI causation. His analogy to earlier automated contract review is offered as experience supporting firms' ability to adapt and retain the value of lawyer expertise. (5) The five-year integration and no-job-loss predictions are his expectations, informed by industry experience and conversations with CIOs and CFOs, rather than labour-market evidence. (6) His strategic-use claim rests on a personal example of an AI tool suggesting a process he found useful.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview distinguishes products introduced around the 2025 conference from a longer-term vision of workflow convergence, explicitly discussed on a five-year horizon.
pts.d: Cartrett describes Ask Matty availability, iTimeKeep Premium and the agentic architecture as current conference-era developments, while seamless cross-application workflows remain a direction of travel without a firm completion date. His broader forecast of product-line convergence and increased employee capacity responds to a five-year question, implying roughly 2030 from the 2025 interview. AI-enabled cloud general-ledger functionality requires Aderant identity and cloud participation through Sierra; only some cloud-native innovations can connect to on-premises systems. He expects cloud GL and AR feature competitiveness around October or November of the interview year, with additional functionality beyond on-premises products, but acknowledges the early-adopter releases are not yet fully equivalent. He places any end of on-premises choice far in the future and promises continuing support. Existing Sierra customers receive core innovations through their subscriptions, whereas heavier premium AI automation requires an additional subscription. Automation retains human review: lawyers review generated time cards and humans can check intermediate workflow steps. His revenue-retention expectation depends on firms adapting pricing and focusing on lawyer skill; it is not an unconditional guarantee of revenue or a dated prediction that hourly billing will end.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are large law firms, their lawyers and business-support teams, Aderant's software customers, and firms' fee-paying clients.
pts.d: Cartrett focuses on large and international firms with complex billing and customised systems, including AmLaw firms. Lawyers are expected to spend less effort entering and correcting time while retaining responsibility for reviewing generated entries and supplying professional judgment. Finance, billing, accounting and other firm professionals would gain integrated workflows, AI-assisted queries and less manual administration. Aderant users and their support counterparts would experience a shift toward self-service troubleshooting rather than repeated support handoffs. CIOs and CFOs face cloud-migration and operational redesign decisions; on-premises customers receive only some of the innovations available to cloud subscribers. Firm employees broadly are framed as becoming more productive rather than being displaced, with no specific occupation-level estimates. Firms could retain some efficiency gains under fixed fees, while clients could receive lower prices than the previous hourly equivalent in Cartrett's illustrative example. Aderant and competing software vendors are also implicated through application convergence, premium AI subscriptions and Cartrett's claimed advantage for integrated billing-data providers over standalone tools. He does not make specific access-to-justice or unmet civil legal need claims.
